title: Greek wonder-tales and Plato’s oath
source_text: Εἶτά φησι μετὰ ἄλλας λέξεις Πλατωνικὰς, δηλούσας ὅτι „ὀλίγοις“ ἐστὶ γνωστὸν τὸ ἀγαθὸν, ἐπεὶ οἱ πολλοὶ μετὰ „καταφρονήσεως οὐκ ὀρθῆς“ „ὑψηλῆς καὶ χαύνης ἐλπίδος“ πληρωθέντες „ὡς σεμνὰ ἄττα“ μεμαθηκότες λέγουσί τινα ὡς ἀληθῆ, ὅτι ταῦτα προειρηκὼς ὁ Πλάτων ὅμως οὐ τερατεύεται οὐδ᾿ ἀποφράττει τοῦ προαιρεῖσθαι βουλομένου, τί ποτε ἐστὶν ὃ ἐπαγγέλλεται, τὴν γλῶτταν, οὐδ᾿ αὐτόθεν κελεύει φθάσαντας πιστεύειν ὅτι τοιόσδε ἐστὶν ὁ θεὸς καὶ υἱὸν ἔχει τοιόνδε, καὶ οὗτος κατελθὼν ἐμοὶ διελέξατο. καὶ πρὸς ταῦτά φημι ὅτι περὶ μὲν Πλάτωνος Ἀρίστανδρος οἶμαι ἀνέγραψεν ὡς οὐκ Ἀρίστωνος υἱοῦ ἀλλὰ φάσματος, ἐν Ἀπόλλωνος εἴδει προσελθόντος τῇ Ἀμφικτιόνῃ· καὶ ἄλλοι δὲ πλείονες τῶν Πλατωνικῶν ἐν τῷ Πλάτωνος βίῳ τοιαῦτ᾿ εἰρήκασι· περὶ δὲ Πυθαγόρου, πλεῖστα ὅσα τερατευσαμένου καὶ δείξαντος μὲν ἐν πανηγύρει Ἑλλήνων ἐλεφάντινον τὸν μηρὸν ἀνεγνωρικέναι δὲ φήσαντος τὴν ἀσπίδα, ᾗ ἐχρῆτο, ὅτ᾿ Εὔφορβος ἦν, καὶ ἐν μιᾷ λεγομένου ἡμέρᾳ ἐν δύο πεφηνέναι πόλεσι, τί χρὴ καὶ λέγειν; ὁ δὲ βουλόμενος κατηγορεῖν ὡς τερατείας ἱστορουμένης περὶ Πλάτωνος καὶ Σωκράτους ἐκθήσεται καὶ τὸν συνιστάμενον Σωκράτει καθ᾿ ὕπνον κύκνον καὶ τὸν διδάσκαλον εἰπόντα ἐπὶ τῇ συστάσει τοῦ νεανίσκου· „οὗτος ἄρα ὁ κύκνος ἦν.“ ἀλλὰ καὶ ὃν τρίτον εἶδεν ὀφθαλμὸν ἑαυτὸν ἔχοντα ὁ Πλάτων εἰς τερατείαν ἀναλήψεται. οὐ λείψει δὲ τοὺς κακοήθεις καὶ κακηγορεῖν βουλομένους τὰ τοῖς κρείττοσι παρὰ τοὺς πολλοὺς ἐπιφανέντα, διαβολὴ καὶ κακηγορία· οἵτινες καὶ τὸ Σωκράτους δαιμόνιον ὡς πλάσμα χλευάσουσιν. οὐ τερατευόμεθα οὖν τὰ περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ διηγούμενοι, οὐδ᾿ οἱ γνήσιοι αὐτοῦ μαθηταὶ τοιούτους ἀνέγραψαν λόγους περὶ αὐτοῦ. ὁ δὲ πάντ᾿ ἐπαγγελλόμενος εἰδέναι Κέλσος καὶ πολλὰ τῶν Πλάτωνος παρατιθέμενος ἑκὼν οἶμαι σιωπᾷ τὸν περὶ υἱοῦ θεοῦ λόγον, τὸν παρὰ Πλάτωνι λελεγμένον ἐν τῇ πρὸς Ἑρμείαν καὶ Κορίσκον ἐπιστολῇ. οὕτω δὲ ἔχει ἡ τοῦ Πλάτωνος λέξις· „καὶ τὸν τῶν πάντων θεὸν ἡγεμόνα τῶν τε ὄντων καὶ τῶν μελλόντων, τοῦ τε ἡγεμονικοῦ καὶ αἰτίου πατέρα καὶ κύριον ἐπομνύντας· ὃν, ἂν ὄντως φιλοσοφῶμεν, εἰσόμεθα πάντες (σαφῶς) εἰς δύναμιν ἀνθρώπων εὐδαιμόνων.“
pass_a_gloss: Then he says after other Platonic phrases (λέξεις) showing that to 'few' (ὀλίγοι) the good (τὸ ἀγαθόν) is known (γνωστόν), since the many, filled with 'contempt (καταφρόνησις) not right (ὀρθή)' and 'lofty (ὑψηλή) and empty (χαῦνος) hope (ἐλπίς)', say some things as true 'as having learned some grand (σεμνά) things', that having said these beforehand Plato nevertheless does not tell marvels (τερατεύομαι) nor block (ἀποφράττω) the tongue of one wishing to choose/judge (προαιρεῖσθαι) what it is he professes (ἐπαγγέλλομαι), nor bids (κελεύω) [them], anticipating, believe at once (αὐτόθεν) that God is such and has such a Son (υἱός), and this one having come down (κατέρχομαι) conversed (διαλέγομαι) with me. To these I say: about Plato Aristander, I think, wrote that [he was] not son of Ariston but of an apparition (φάσμα) having come to Amphictione in Apollo's form (εἶδος); and more others of the Platonists said such in the Life of Plato; about Pythagoras, who told very many marvels and showed at a festival (πανήγυρις) of Greeks his ivory (ἐλεφάντινος) thigh (μηρός) and said he had recognized (ἀναγνωρίζω) the shield (ἀσπίς) he used when he was Euphorbus, and is said on one day to have appeared (φαίνομαι) in two cities, what need to say? One wishing to accuse (κατηγορέω) as wonder-mongering (τερατεία) narrated about Plato and Socrates will set out the swan (κύκνος) commended/introduced (συνίστημι) to Socrates in sleep (ὕπνος) and the teacher saying at the introduction (σύστασις) of the youth (νεανίσκος): 'this then was the swan'. Also the third eye (ὀφθαλμός) which Plato saw himself having he will take up as wonder-mongering. Slander (διαβολή) and abuse (κακηγορία) will not fail the malicious (κακοήθεις) wishing to revile things that appeared to the better (κρείττονες) beyond the many; who will also mock (χλευάζω) Socrates's daimonion (δαιμόνιον) as a fiction (πλάσμα). We do not then tell marvels narrating about Jesus, nor did his genuine (γνήσιοι) disciples write such accounts (λόγοι) about him. Celsus professing to know all and citing (παρατίθημι) many of Plato's, willingly (ἑκών), I think, keeps silent about the account (λόγος) about the Son of God said in Plato in the letter to Hermias and Coriscus. Plato's phrase: 'and swearing (ἐπόμνυμι) by the God of all, leader (ἡγεμών) of things that are and will be, and father and lord (πατήρ, κύριος) of the ruling principle (ἡγεμονικόν) and cause (αἴτιον); whom, if we truly (ὄντως) philosophize, we shall all know (οἶδα) clearly to the power of blessed (εὐδαίμονες) men.'
pass_b_english: Then, after other passages of Plato showing that the good is known to “few,” because the many, filled “with a contempt that is not right” and “with a lofty and empty hope,” speak of certain things as true “as though they had learned something grand” (Plato, Seventh Letter 341e), he says that Plato, though he had said this beforehand, still does not tell tales of wonder, nor does he stop the tongue of anyone who wishes to weigh what it is that he professes, nor does he bid people believe straight away: “God is of such a kind, and he has a Son of such a kind, and this Son came down and talked with me.”

To this I reply that Aristander, I think, wrote of Plato that he was not the son of Ariston but of an apparition that came to Amphictione in the form of Apollo; and many other Platonists have said such things in their accounts of Plato’s life. And as for Pythagoras, who told a great many marvels, who showed his ivory thigh at a festival gathering of the Greeks, who claimed he recognized the shield he had used when he was Euphorbus, and who is said to have appeared in two cities on one day, what need is there even to speak?

Anyone who wants to charge that tales of wonder are told about Plato and Socrates will cite the swan that was presented to Socrates in a dream, and the teacher who said, when the young man was presented to him, “So this was the swan.” He will also take up as a tale of wonder the third eye that Plato saw he himself had. Malicious people, who wish to speak evil of what has appeared to those who stand above the many, will never lack slander and abuse; they will also mock the divine sign of Socrates as a fiction.

We, then, are not telling tales of wonder when we relate the things about Jesus, and his true disciples did not write such stories about him. But Celsus, who professes to know everything and quotes many passages of Plato, deliberately, I think, keeps silent about the teaching on the Son of God that is stated by Plato in the letter to Hermias and Coriscus. Plato’s words run thus: “and swearing by the God of all things, leader of what is and of what is to be, Father and Lord of the ruling principle and cause; whom, if we truly practise philosophy, we shall all know clearly, as far as is possible for blessed human beings” (Plato, Sixth Letter 323d).

choices.choice: Plato, Seventh Letter 341e: the quoted Platonic phrases (‘few’, ‘contempt not right’, ‘lofty and empty hope’, ‘as though they had learned something grand’); Celsus’s own claims are reported indirectly by Origen and are kept as reported speech, while the mocking direct-speech slogan (‘God is of such a kind... talked with me’) is put in quotation marks. προαιρεῖσθαι (‘to choose’) is awkward with ‘what it is he professes’; rendered ‘to weigh’ as the nearest sense, possibly a corrupt reading (a verb of asking would fit better, but no emendation is made here). ‘Amphictione’ is the name in the text (Plato’s mother is elsewhere Perictione); kept as written. The text says ‘ivory thigh’; the usual tradition says golden, but the text is translated as given. Aristander and the swan and third-eye stories are not given inline sources: the swan dream is told in later Lives of Plato (e.g. Diogenes Laertius 3.5), but no source is cited inline since the exact source Origen used is uncertain. δαιμόνιον of Socrates rendered ‘divine sign’, the usual English name for it. ἐκθήσεται is future and is rendered ‘will cite’ to match ἀναλήψεται (‘will take up’). The closing quotation is Plato, Sixth Letter 323d (to Hermias, Erastus and Coriscus); ’(clearly)’ (σαφῶς) is an editorial supplement in the edition and is translated. The text here reads τοῦ ἡγεμονικοῦ (‘the ruling principle’), not Plato’s τοῦ ἡγεμόνος (‘the leader’), and is translated as given. ‘The God of all things’, ‘leader’ and ‘Father and Lord’ are all in apposition to one object of the oath, so no second ‘by’ is supplied. Origen reads the God of all and the Father and Lord as the true God, so they are capitalized; ‘the ruling principle and cause’, which he takes of the Son, is kept lowercase as Plato’s words. No Scripture is quoted in this chapter.
ἐκθήσεται (future): 'would set out' changed to 'will cite', matching 'will take up'
Sixth Letter quotation: removed the second 'by', which made the Father and Lord a separate object of the oath; the Greek has one object in apposition
